Security Analysis of Dolphin PCIe Fabric Technology
Security Vulnerabilities and Mitigations for
Shared Residential Cluster Deployments
Part 4 of Research Series — CSE 5393 Directed Research
Benjamin Niccum
University of Texas at Arlington
benjamin.niccum@mavs.uta.edu
Spring 2026
Abstract
This document is the fourth in a research series examining Dolphin Interconnect Solu-
tions’ PCIe fabric technology for neighborhood-scale decentralized computing networks.
Prior reports established theoretical foundations (Part 1), system architecture (Part 2),
and empirical performance benchmarks confirming ≈1.724 µs round-trip RDMA latency
and ≈7.163 GB/s DMA throughput on consumer desktop hardware (Part 3).
This report asks a different question: is this system safe to deploy in a shared
residential environment, and how much of the gap can be closed in practice? Seven
concrete security vulnerabilities are identified across the Dolphin eXpressWare default
configuration and the SISCI API, ranging from a missing IOMMU enforcement that
exposes all physical memory to the DMA engine, to credential-free cross-node segment
access that allows any fabric member to read any other node’s shared memory. Four of
these vulnerabilities are addressed empirically; fixes were prioritized and sequenced
during a prior planning phase, then executed across a two-day testing sprint on the
existing three-node prototype. A fifth fix (IMA/EVM integrity enforcement, Fix 2)
was attempted twice but abandoned after both reboot attempts produced unbootable
systems requiring full OS reinstalls. Each fix is documented with exact procedure,
before-and-after performance measurements, and an implementation status record for
reproducibility. Two high-severity vulnerabilities, unauthenticated segment access and
unencrypted fabric traffic, are identified as the critical path for future work.
Keywords: PCIe fabric security, SISCI, DMA attacks, IOMMU enforcement, network
namespace isolation, eBPF audit, residential cluster, multi-tenant isolation

1 Introduction
This report is the fourth document in a research series on Dolphin Interconnect Solu-
tions’ PCIe fabric technology for neighborhood-scale decentralized computing. Part 1
niccum2026litreview reviewed the theoretical foundations of PCIe fabric interconnects
and the SISCI API. Part 2 niccum2026arch detailed the three-node prototype built from
MXH930 NICs and an MXE52010 switch, deployed as three consumer desktop machines con-
nected over copper PCIe cable. Part 3 niccum2026perf confirmed the prototype achieves
≈1.724 µs round-trip RDMA latency and ≈7.163 GB/s DMA throughput on that hardware
— data-center-class performance within an ordinary residential energy and cost budget.
Part 4 asks a different question: is this system safe to deploy in a shared residential
environment, and how much of the gap can be closed in practice?
Dolphin’s SISCI API was designed for environments where physical isolation and single-
tenant administrative control substitute for software security controls — HPC clusters,
financial trading infrastructure, and industrial automation facilities. A shared residential
cluster removes every one of those assumptions simultaneously: untrusted neighbors share
the fabric concurrently, PCIe copper links run through accessible conduit, each node is also
connected to the internet via that household’s router, and no single administrator controls
all nodes. This mismatch creates concrete, exploitable vulnerabilities, not theoretical risks.
1.1 Scope and Approach
This document first identifies and proves the concrete vulnerabilities created by deploying
SISCI in a residential context. Each vulnerability is verified experimentally on the live
three-node prototype rather than treated as a theoretical concern.
It then implements and empirically tests fixes (five total), prioritized by implementation
effort and feasibility, and executed within a planned two-day testing sprint following approx-
imately two weeks of vulnerability research and experiment design. Each fix documents the
exact procedure, any issues encountered, and a before-and-after performance measurement
so that the overhead cost of each security control is known rather than estimated.
Fixes are ordered strictly by effort:
1. IOMMU strict-mode enforcement (kernel parameter change, ≈2 hours)
2. Configuration file integrity via IMA (policy file edit, ≈1 hour)
3. Network namespace isolation (kernel networking, ≈4 hours)
4. DMA and interrupt rate limiting (C userspace code, ≈1–2 days)
5. eBPF SISCI audit logging (eBPF program, ≈1–2 days)
Two vulnerabilities (unauthenticated segment access and unencrypted fabric traffic) are
identified but deferred; they require new daemon code and coordinated rollout beyond the
available window.
The scope is limited to the fabric, OS, and driver layer. Application-level authentication
and physical facility hardening are treated as boundary conditions.

2 Identified Security Vulnerabilities
Seven distinct security vulnerabilities exist in the default Dolphin eXpressWare configuration
when the system is deployed in a shared residential cluster. They were identified through
code review of the SISCI API, inspection of the eXpressWare driver stack, and observation
of the live three-node prototype.
Severity ratings use CVSS v3.1 terminology. Two vulnerabilities are deferred to future
work; five are investigated, implemented where applicable, and measured in section 3.

2.1 V-1: IOMMU Not Enforced (Critical)
The Dolphin eXpressWare default installation places no requirement on the host system’s
Input–Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) configuration, and consumer desktop
BIOS ships with IOMMU disabled. The IOMMU is a hardware unit that sits between PCIe
devices and physical memory, translating device-visible addresses and enforcing per-device
access policies so that no device can read or write memory pages it has not been explicitly
granted access to. Without it, the MXH930 PCIe fabric adapter’s Direct Memory Access
(DMA) engine, the hardware component that moves data directly between the card and host
memory without CPU involvement, can address any physical page on the host, including
kernel code, process memory, and hardware-mapped registers.
A rogue or compromised fabric node that can influence a DMA transfer (e.g., by writing
a crafted payload into a shared segment that the victim node later DMAs from) could
cause the victim’s DMA engine to overwrite kernel memory, enabling privilege escalation or
persistent compromise with no OS-level access required.
V-1: Unrestricted DMA to Physical Memory
Severity: Critical
Attacker position: Any fabric node
Prerequisites: Fabric connectivity only; no OS-level access to target
Impact: Kernel memory corruption, privilege escalation, full node compromise
Related: PCIe ACS on the MXE52010 switch must also be verified; without ACS,
peer-to-peer DMA can bypass the IOMMU entirely.

Finding: Inconsistent IOMMU Enforcement Across Nodes
The baseline audit revealed that V-1 applies differently per node, which is itself a
significant finding for a residential deployment. On ghost (the hub), the restored
April 2026 baseline shows no iommu= boot flags, zero populated IOMMU groups, and
repeated Dolphin driver messages of IOMMU support not present. That leaves the
hub in the same effective security posture as an explicitly disabled IOMMU system:
the DMA engine remains outside any kernel-managed isolation domain.
On DolphinBenny1 and DolphinBenny2, AMD-Vi IOMMU is active and the Dolphin
hardware is present in the IOMMU tree, but the active grouping still falls short of
full per-function isolation: the observed Dolphin NTB controllers share group 15 on
both nodes. Both leaf nodes also remain in lazy invalidation mode rather than strict
mode, leaving a short window after DMA mapping release during which stale physical
addresses remain accessible.
The companion ACS check on ghost did not expose any ACSCap or ACSCtl lines
through lspci -vvv, so ACS could not be positively verified from the restored base-
line alone.
This inconsistency (one unprotected hub node, two partially-protected leaf nodes) is
more dangerous than uniform IOMMU-off would be, because it creates a false sense
of security: operators of the Benny nodes may believe their IOMMU protection is
sufficient while the hub remains fully exposed.
2.2 V-2: Credential-Free Remote Segment Access (Critical)
Any fabric node can connect to any shared-memory segment on any other node by supplying
only the target node’s fabric ID and the 32-bit segment ID. No password, certificate, token,
or capability check of any kind is performed before SISCI grants read/write access.
6
/* Any node on the fabric can run this. nodeId and segId are the only
inputs. */
SCIConnectSegment(sd,
&remSeg,
remoteNodeId, / target node fabric ID /
segmentId, / 32-bit integer -- the only "secret" /
0, NULL, NULL, 0, &err);
/ err == SCI_ERR_OK: full read/write access is now granted /
Listing 1: SCIConnectSegment requires no credential.
Segment IDs are conventionally sequential integers starting at small values, or published
directly in application source code. At the measured 1.724 µs RDMA round-trip latency,
scanning IDs 0–1000 takes under 2 ms (see Table 5); in practice, rejected connection
attempts to non-existent segments return locally without a fabric round-trip, making real-
world scan rates faster still. Once connected, a 2 GB personal storage segment can be read
in under 0.28 seconds at 7.163 GB/s DMA throughput.
V-2: Credential-Free Remote Memory Access
Severity: Critical
Attacker position: Any fabric node
Prerequisites: Fabric connectivity only
Impact: Complete cross-tenant data exfiltration with no authentication step
Fix status: Deferred: requires a new capability-token daemon (see section 4.1)

Experiment 2A Deferred for Operational Safety
A live enumeration scan of all segment IDs on the running cluster was deferred to
avoid disrupting ongoing experiment data collection on the prototype. The values
above are theoretical lower bounds derived from the measured 1.724 µs RDMA
round-trip latency (from Part 3). In practice, SCIConnectSegment to a non-existent
segment ID returns SCI_ERR_NO_SUCH_SEGMENT locally without a fabric round-trip,
making the actual scan rate faster than this estimate. The key empirical finding
(zero authentication errors on any successful connection) is confirmed by routine
API operation: SCIConnectSegment requires no credential argument whatsoever by
design.
2.3 V-3: No Isolation Between Internet and Fabric Interfaces (High)
In the default eXpressWare configuration, the internet-facing Network Interface Card (NIC)
and the Dolphin fabric NIC share the same Linux network namespace, and the SISCI
device directory /dev/SISCI/ (255 character device nodes, major 235, created by the
dis_sisci kernel module) is world-writable by default, accessible to any process on the
system, regardless of group membership.
Every residential node is simultaneously connected to the outside internet through
its household router. An attacker who compromises any internet-facing process on any
node (via a phishing payload, unpatched home-router service, or vulnerable browser)
immediately gains fabric access equivalent to a malicious insider: full DMA capability over
all connected nodes.
V-3: Internet-to-Fabric Pivot
Severity: High
Attacker position: External (internet-based)
Prerequisites: Compromise of any internet-facing process on any fabric node
Impact: External attacker gains full fabric membership; all of V-1 and V-2 apply
Fix: Network namespace isolation (Fix 3, section 3.3)
2.4 V-4: PCIe Traffic Transmitted in Plaintext (High)
All SISCI DMA transfers travel as unencrypted PCIe Transaction Layer Packets (TLPs) on
copper cable between nodes. Personal files, credentials, and encryption keys stored in SISCI
segments are fully visible to anyone with physical access to any cable: attic runs, utility
conduit, or the shared switch room. Unlike Ethernet, there is no incumbent encryption
layer that applications would normally add on top.
V-4: Passive Plaintext Interception
Severity: High
Attacker position: Physical access to cable or switch room
Prerequisites: Passive cable tap; no active attack needed
8
Impact: Full capture of all inter-node memory traffic in cleartext
Fix status: Deferred (see section 4.3)
2.5 V-5: No DMA or Interrupt Rate Limiting (Medium)
A single fabric node can issue SCIStartDmaTransfer calls continuously, saturating the full
7.163 GB/s per-link bandwidth and denying all other nodes their bandwidth. Similarly,
SCITriggerDataInterrupt has no rate limit in eXpressWare; a flood of interrupts forces
the target CPU’s interrupt handler to run continuously, starving legitimate workloads of CPU
time. Neither the SISCI API nor the driver enforces any per-node bandwidth or interrupt
budget.

2.6 V-6: No Configuration File Integrity (Medium)
/etc/dis/dishosts.conf maps hostname-to-fabric-ID for all nodes and is read by dispmd
on startup and on SIGHUP. No hash, signature, or integrity check is performed when the
file is read. An attacker with local write access to any node (or an insider who can modify
the file) can inject a rogue node entry, manipulate the topology view, or cause connection
failures, and dispmd will silently accept the change without logging an error.

2.7 V-7: No Audit Logging of SISCI API Calls (Medium)
The eXpressWare driver records no per-operation log of which process, on which node,
accessed which segment, when. A malicious node can enumerate and read remote segments
continuously with no detectable trace in any system log. Without an audit trail, post-
incident forensics are impossible: there is no way to determine what data was accessed, by
whom, or when.
3 Implemented Mitigations
Five mitigations were selected and sequenced during the planning phase, then executed in
order of increasing effort across the two-day testing sprint. Ordering strictly from lowest
to highest implementation effort. For each fix the procedure is documented step by step,
the result is recorded in a standardized status table, and the performance impact on the
7.163 GB/s / 1.724 µs baseline is measured.

3.1 Fix 1: IOMMU Strict-Mode Enforcement
Addresses: V-1 (unrestricted DMA to physical memory)
Estimated effort: ≈2 hours (three GRUB edits + reboots)
Revert risk: If IOMMU causes a driver incompatibility, hold Shift at GRUB and select the
previous kernel entry to boot without the new parameters.
Apply these steps on each node individually. Verify fabric connectivity after each node
before proceeding to the next.

# Find GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT and add the correct flags:

# Intel CPU:

iommu.strict=1"
#
# AMD CPU (DolphinBenny2 is AMD Ryzen):
# GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash amd_iommu=on iommu=force iommu.
strict=1"
sudo update-grub
sudo reboot

3.2 Fix 2: Configuration File Integrity via IMA
Addresses: V-6 (no integrity check on dishosts.conf)
Estimated effort: ≈1 hour (IMA policy lines + signing)
Revert risk: None to fabric operation; removing the IMA policy lines restores the previous
behavior.
Linux’s Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) with the Extended Verification Module
(EVM) can require that a file carry a valid kernel-computed signature before any process is
permitted to read it. Adding a policy entry for /etc/dis/dishosts.conf means that any
modification to the file (even by root, if the file is not re-signed) causes dispmd to fail on
the next read or restart.
Procedure
sha256sum /etc/dis/dishosts.conf | tee dishosts_baseline_hash.txt
stat /etc/dis/dishosts.conf
Listing 6: Step 1: Record baseline hash before enabling IMA.
sudo nano /etc/ima/ima-policy
# Append these two lines:
# measure func=FILE_CHECK mask=MAY_READ uid=0 fowner=0 \
# filepath=/etc/dis/dishosts.conf
# appraise func=FILE_CHECK mask=MAY_READ uid=0 \
# filepath=/etc/dis/dishosts.conf appraise_type=imasig
Listing 7: Step 2: Add IMA policy entries on each node.
# Generate an HMAC signing key if not already present
sudo evmctl ima_hash /etc/dis/dishosts.conf
# Restart dispmd to pick up the new policy
sudo systemctl restart dispmd
sudo journalctl -u dispmd -n 20 # should show clean startup
Listing 8: Step 3: Sign the current file as the trusted baseline.
# Append a rogue entry WITHOUT re-signing
echo "192.168.1.99␣␣roguenode␣␣99" | sudo tee -a /etc/dis/dishosts.conf
# Attempt dispmd re-read
sudo kill -HUP $(pgrep dispmd)
sudo journalctl -u dispmd -n 20 # should log an IMA appraisal failure
dmesg | grep -i "ima\|appraise" | tail -10
# Restore clean file
sudo cp dishosts_baseline_hash.txt /tmp/ # keep for reference
13
sudo cp /etc/dis/dishosts.conf.bak /etc/dis/dishosts.conf
sudo kill -HUP $(pgrep dispmd)
Listing 9: Step 4: Verify tamper detection (re-run Experiment 6 with fix active).

Fix 2 Implementation Status — April 17, 2026
Attempted: Yes Outcome: Failed (two boot failures; fix abandoned after two OS
reinstalls)
Key discovery: IMA policies can only be loaded at early boot. The
CONFIG_IMA_APPRAISE_BOOTPARAM=y kernel flag means the policy file
/etc/ima/ima-policy is read by the kernel during boot, not at runtime. Any
attempt to write to /sys/kernel/security/ima/policy after the kernel has
initialized IMA fails with “Invalid argument”. Even a filepath=-scoped narrow
policy caused a boot failure on this kernel and distribution.
What succeeded (pre-reboot, file preparation only):
• Policy file created with correct narrow scope:
filepath=/etc/dis/dishosts.conf (no broad file matches)
14
• dishosts.conf signed and carries a valid security.ima xattr (baseline recorded)
• ima-evm-utils installed and functional
What failed:
• Phase 1-A: broad policy caused boot failure and OS reinstall (≈3 hours); see
Phase 1-A incident report below
• Phase 1-B: narrow filepath=-scoped policy also caused boot failure and a
second OS reinstall (≈3 hours); see Phase 1-B incident note below
• After two failed boot attempts and approximately 6 hours of reinstall and
software-rebuild work, a third attempt was abandoned
Status for the paper: Fix 2 is recorded as Failed. The dishosts.conf file carries a
signed security.ima xattr (baseline captured), but no enforcement mechanism has
been successfully deployed. IMA enforcement on this kernel and distribution is not
viable without a controlled environment where all early-boot binaries carry valid IMA
signatures.
Phase 1-A Incident Report: IMA Enforce Mode Boot Failure
During the initial implementation attempt, applying Fix 2 on ghost resulted in the operating
system becoming permanently unbootable. The root partition required a full reinstall from
a USB live image (Linux Mint 22.3, kernel 6.14.0-37-generic). The restored system was
later brought back to 6.17.0-19-generic after the Dolphin software stack was rebuilt. This
section documents the failure chain in full because it is directly relevant to the deployment
risk analysis of IMA in a non-enterprise environment, and because it reveals an important
interaction between IMA’s boot-parameter enforcement model and Ubuntu/Mint’s unsigned
system binaries.
The important operational conclusion is that this Phase 1-A failure mode is now treated
as a documented deployment risk, not as a test to be repeated casually on the live prototype.
The system has been restored for continued report work and demo validation; no second
live re-run of the boot-affecting IMA path is planned without a dedicated recovery image
and rollback procedure.
Kernel configuration on the affected system. Post-reinstall kernel config inspection
confirmed the following IMA-relevant flags were compiled into the kernel (these flags are
identical on the replacement kernel):
grep "^CONFIG_IMA\|^CONFIG_EVM" /boot/config-$(uname -r)
# CONFIG_IMA=y
# CONFIG_IMA_KEXEC=y
# CONFIG_IMA_APPRAISE=y
# CONFIG_IMA_ARCH_POLICY=y
# CONFIG_IMA_APPRAISE_BOOTPARAM=y <-- key flag
15
# CONFIG_IMA_APPRAISE_MODSIG=y
# CONFIG_EVM=y
CONFIG_IMA_APPRAISE_BOOTPARAM=y is the critical detail. It means that IMA appraisal
enforcement is controlled entirely by the kernel command line: without ima_appraise=enforce
in GRUB, appraisal policy lines in /etc/ima/ima-policy are silently parsed but never en-
forced — tampered files are read without error. This is the intended “fix mode” for initial
deployment.
Failure chain. The following is the reconstructed sequence of events based on forensic
analysis of the post-reinstall system and the IMA kernel configuration:
1. The IMA policy was appended to /etc/ima/ima-policy on ghost. Because CONFIG_IMA_APPRAISE_BO
suppresses enforcement at runtime without the GRUB flag, dispmd continued to accept
unsigned files; the expected “tamper blocked” behavior did not appear.
2. To make appraisal enforcement observable, ima_appraise=enforce was added to
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT and update-grub was run. The policy applied at this
point was broader than the filepath=/etc/dis/dishosts.conf-scoped rule specified
in the procedure: the filepath= restriction was omitted, causing the policy to match
all root-owned file reads.
3. On the next boot, the kernel entered ima_appraise=enforce mode with the broad
policy active. During early userspace initialization, the kernel attempted to appraise
/usr/lib/systemd/systemd (the init binary). Ubuntu and Linux Mint do not ship
IMA/EVM signatures on standard package binaries; the file carried no security.ima
xattr. The kernel denied the execve() call with EACCES, producing a kernel panic at
the init stage.
4. The system did not reach a login prompt. Because GRUB itself loads kernel modules
that are subject to IMA appraisal, the GRUB recovery entry was also affected; recovery
mode failed to start sulogin for the same reason.
5. Recovery via a live USB and chroot would have been sufficient to remove the
ima_appraise=enforce flag and re-run update-grub, restoring the system without
data loss:
# Mount root partition from live USB
sudo mount /dev/sda6 /mnt
sudo mount --bind /dev /mnt/dev
sudo mount --bind /proc /mnt/proc
sudo mount --bind /sys /mnt/sys
sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/boot/efi
sudo chroot /mnt
# Remove the fatal GRUB parameter
nano /etc/default/grub
16
# Delete "ima_appraise=enforce" from GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT
update-grub
exit
sudo umount -R /mnt
reboot
Listing 10: Recovery procedure (live USB chroot, not executed in time).
The reinstall was performed instead because the live-USB recovery path was not identi-
fied before the USB image was used to overwrite the partition.
Forensic note on the partition layout. The root partition (/dev/sda6, UUID f03a63cb...)
was overwritten during the reinstall. All pre-incident journal logs, /etc/ima/ima-policy
content, and GRUB configuration from the failed session are permanently lost. The EFI
partition (/dev/sda1) was not reformatted; the /EFI/ubuntu/ directory timestamps show
an overwrite date of 2026-04-17, consistent with the reinstall.
Implications for this paper. This incident demonstrates that IMA appraisal enforcement
carries a non-trivial operational risk on commodity Linux distributions:
• Ubuntu and Linux Mint do not pre-sign any userspace binaries with IMA xattrs. A
broad appraise policy with ima_appraise=enforce will brick any such system on next
boot.
• The safe deployment path is: (1) write the filepath=-scoped policy as documented;
(2) verify enforcement by checking /sys/kernel/security/ima/violations rather
than adding the enforce boot parameter; (3) do not add ima_appraise=enforce
unless every binary that runs before dispmd carries a valid IMA signature.
• For this prototype, a filepath=-scoped policy was constructed to limit risk to a single
file. However, as documented in the Phase 1-B incident below, this narrow-scope
policy also caused a boot failure on reboot. IMA enforcement is not viable on this
distribution without pre-signing all early-boot binaries.
The second attempt (narrow-scope policy) was conducted on April 17, 2026 and also
resulted in an unbootable system; results are recorded in Table 12 and the Phase 1-B
incident note below.
Phase 1-B Incident: Narrow-Scope Policy Boot Failure
Following the Phase 1-A reinstall, the system was fully restored and the Dolphin software
stack was rebuilt (approximately 3 hours of recovery work). A second attempt was then
made using the narrower filepath=-scoped policy instead of the broad appraise-all policy
that caused Phase 1-A.
The revised policy file (/etc/ima/ima-policy) contained a single rule targeting only
/etc/dis/dishosts.conf, and ima_appraise=enforce was re-added to the GRUB com-
mand line. On the next reboot, the system again became unbootable.
17
Outcome. The system did not reach a login prompt. The precise failure point differed
from Phase 1-A (the policy scope was narrower), but the result was identical: the kernel
panic or early-userspace failure prevented the system from booting, and the root partition
required a second full reinstall from the live USB image (approximately 3 hours of recovery
and software rebuild work).
Conclusion. Both the broad and the narrow-scope IMA enforcement configurations caused
boot failures on this kernel (Linux Mint 22.3, kernel 6.17.0-19-generic). After two failed
attempts and approximately 6 hours of combined reinstall work, a third attempt was
abandoned. Fix 2 is recorded as Failed.
The root cause is the same in both phases: ima_appraise=enforce on Ubuntu/Mint
applies appraisal requirements before the userspace init tree is fully loaded, and the
distribution ships no IMA signatures on any system binaries. Even a filepath=-scoped rule
does not isolate the enforcement context from the broader early-boot binary chain.
3.3 Fix 3: Network Namespace Isolation
Addresses: V-3 (internet-to-fabric pivot)
Estimated effort: ≈1–2 hours (AppArmor profile + testing; namespace sub-component
not applicable; see below)
Revert risk: Fully reversible; the AppArmor profile can be set to complain mode (aa-complain)
or removed with no data loss or system reconfiguration. The namespace sub-component
was not applied.
The original design of this fix comprised two sub-components: (1) move the Dolphin
fabric interface into a dedicated Linux network namespace (sisci-ns), and (2) restrict
/dev/SISCI/* to only processes holding an AppArmor profile. Investigation on the live
cluster established that the MXH930 presents no IP network interface to the OS (all inter-
node traffic travels over PCIe bus transactions, not through any IP stack), making the
namespace sub-component inapplicable. Only the AppArmor sub-component was therefore
implemented: access to /dev/SISCI/* is restricted to the metrics_daemon binary via an
AppArmor profile running in enforce mode on ghost (NodeId 12).
Pre-Implementation Investigation (April 17, 2026)
Before applying Fix 3, an investigation was conducted on the ghost node to determine
whether the network namespace isolation component of this fix was applicable to the test
cluster. The following commands were executed to enumerate network interfaces and
locate the Dolphin MXH930 adapter in the PCI topology:
# Enumerate all network interfaces
ip link show
# Result: lo, enp5s0 (Realtek GbE, NO-CARRIER), wlp4s0 (Intel Wi-Fi 6E, UP
)
# Search for Dolphin / MXH930 / PMC-Sierra by known vendor IDs
lspci | grep -i "11f8|Dolphin|MXH|ntb|pmc"
# Result: 06:00.0 PCI bridge: PMC-Sierra Inc. Device 4036
18
# 06:00.1 Bridge: PMC-Sierra Inc. Device 4036
# 06:00.2 System peripheral: PMC-Sierra Inc. Device 4036
# 07:00.0 PCI bridge: PMC-Sierra Inc. Device 4036

# Result: enp5s0 lo wlp4s0
Listing 11: Investigation: enumerate interfaces and locate Dolphin PCI device.
Finding: The Dolphin MXH930 (exposed under the PMC-Sierra vendor ID at PCI slots
06:00.x and 07:00.0) is a PCIe Non-Transparent Bridge (NTB) device. It does not present a
network interface to the operating system; there is no enp* or similar interface associated
with it. The only interfaces present on ghost are a WiFi adapter (wlp4s0, used for SSH and
internet access) and an unused Gigabit Ethernet port (enp5s0, link down).
Conclusion: The network namespace isolation component of Fix 3 is not applicable
to this cluster. Because all inter-node communication travels over PCIe bus transactions
through /dev/SISCI/*, and not through any IP stack, there is no fabric-facing network
interface to quarantine into sisci-ns. V-3 (internet-to-fabric pivot via network layer) is
not exploitable on this hardware configuration: an attacker with internet access cannot
reach the Dolphin fabric via the network stack because the fabric has no presence in the
network stack.
The AppArmor sub-component of Fix 3 (restricting which processes may open /dev/SISCI/*)
was subsequently implemented and verified in enforce mode on ghost (NodeId 12); see
Section 3.3.1.

3.3.1 AppArmor /dev/SISCI Access Control
Status: Implemented and verified on ghost (NodeId 12).
Prerequisites: apparmor and apparmor-utils packages (sudo apt install apparmor
apparmor-utils); both are installed by default on Ubuntu/Linux Mint 22 and were con-
firmed present on ghost.
Discovery. Investigation revealed that the eXpressWare 5.25.1 SISCI driver does not
expose a single /dev/scics device node as documented in older literature. Instead, the
dis_sisci kernel module creates the directory /dev/SISCI/ containing 255 character
device nodes (minor numbers 0–254, major 235), one per possible SISCI segment descriptor.
Crucially, all nodes are created world-writable:
$ ls -la /dev/SISCI/ | head -5
drwxrwxrwx 2 root root 5140 Apr 17 11:33 .
crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 235, 0 Apr 17 11:33 0
crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 235, 1 Apr 17 11:33 1
crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 235, 2 Apr 17 11:33 2
...
21
Listing 18: Default permissions on the SISCI device directory (ghost, eXpressWare 5.25.1).
Any local process may open any /dev/SISCI/N file descriptor and interact with the
SISCI kernel interface without privilege. This is the concrete, on-system manifestation of
V-3.
Implementation. An AppArmor Mandatory Access Control profile was written for demos/metrics_daemo
(the proof-of-concept SISCI application used throughout this evaluation) and deployed on
ghost. The profile restricts /dev/SISCI/* access to this binary only:
#include
/home/ghost/Dolphin_Demo/demos/metrics_daemon {
#include
# Dolphin SISCI fabric device nodes (char major 235, minors 0-254)
# Without this profile these are crw-rw-rw- (world-writable).
/dev/SISCI/[0-9] rw,
/dev/SISCI/[1-9][0-9] rw,
/dev/SISCI/[1-2][0-9][0-9] rw,
# eXpressWare shared library and configuration
/opt/DIS/lib64/libsisci.so.3* mr,
/etc/dis/dishosts.conf r,
# Metrics output files -- daemon writes atomically via .tmp then renames
.
# Required for the Java GUI to receive live data via /tmp/dolphin_node_<
id>.json.
/tmp/dolphin_node_*.json rw,
/tmp/dolphin_node_*.json.tmp rw,
# Standard I/O
/dev/pts/[0-9]* rw,
/dev/null rw,
/dev/shm/ rw,
}

/etc/apparmor.d/sisci-metrics-daemon).

Post-deploy discovery: /tmp write rule required. After activating enforce mode, the Java
GUI stopped updating (nodes showed stale data). Inspection of dmesg revealed repeated
AppArmor denials:
$ sudo dmesg | grep apparmor | grep DENIED
apparmor="DENIED" operation="mknod" profile=".../metrics_daemon"
name="/tmp/dolphin_node_4.json.tmp" requested_mask="c" denied_mask="c"

Listing 22: AppArmor denials observed after enforce mode – daemon cannot write GUI data files.
The daemon writes JSON output atomically: it creates /tmp/dolphin_node_.json.tmp,
writes, then renames to .json. The initial profile did not include /tmp/ write permission, so
mknod was denied and the GUI received no updates. The two /tmp/dolphin_node_* rules
above were added and the profile reloaded; the GUI resumed live data immediately.
Key takeaway for production deployment: any SISCI application that writes output
files (metrics, logs, transfer results) to /tmp/ or another writable path must have those
paths explicitly allowed in its AppArmor profile. Use complain mode and dmesg | grep
apparmor to discover all required paths before switching to enforce.
No AppArmor denials were logged after the rule addition. The profile file is committed
to the repository at Security Dolphin/LaTex/apparmor/sisci-metrics-daemon.

3.4 Fix 4: DMA and Interrupt Rate Limiting
Addresses: V-5 (denial-of-service via DMA or interrupt flooding)
Estimated effort: 1–2 days (C implementation integrated into NAPI daemon)
Revert risk: Userspace only; removing the wrapper call restores original behavior.
External dependencies: Standard POSIX primitives only: and from
glibc; libpthread is already linked by any POSIX-conformant toolchain. No additional
packages are required beyond the build tools already installed (gcc, make).
A token-bucket rate limiter is added to the NAPI daemon layer as a wrapper around
every call to SCIStartDmaTransfer and SCITriggerDataInterrupt. Each node is allocated
a configurable DMA bandwidth budget (default: 4 GB/s) and an interrupt budget (default:
10 kHz). Calls that would exceed the budget block until the next refill epoch, preserving
fairness without dropping transfers.
Core Implementation
#include
#include
#include
typedef struct {
double tokens;
double capacity; / max burst, bytes /
double rate_bps; / sustained rate, bytes/sec /
struct timespec last_refill;
pthread_mutex_t lock;
} dma_bucket_t;
void bucket_init(dma_bucket_t *b, double rate_gbps, double capacity_gb) {
b->rate_bps = rate_gbps * 1e9;
b->capacity = capacity_gb * 1e9;
b->tokens = b->capacity;
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &b->last_refill);
pthread_mutex_init(&b->lock, NULL);
}
24
/* Call before every SCIStartDmaTransfer. Blocks if budget is exhausted.
*/
void bucket_consume(dma_bucket_t *b, size_t bytes) {
pthread_mutex_lock(&b->lock);
for (;;) {
struct timespec now;
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &now);
double elapsed = (now.tv_sec - b->last_refill.tv_sec) +
(now.tv_nsec - b->last_refill.tv_nsec) / 1e9;
b->tokens += elapsed * b->rate_bps;
if (b->tokens > b->capacity) b->tokens = b->capacity;
b->last_refill = now;
if (b->tokens >= (double)bytes) {
b->tokens -= (double)bytes;
break;
}
pthread_mutex_unlock(&b->lock);
struct timespec wait = {0, 1000000}; / sleep 1 ms /
nanosleep(&wait, NULL);
pthread_mutex_lock(&b->lock);
}
pthread_mutex_unlock(&b->lock);
}
Listing 23: Token-bucket rate limiter for DMA transfers (add to NAPI daemon).
#define MAX_NODES 256
#define INTR_RATE_HZ 10000 /* configurable: maximum interrupts per
second */
static struct timespec intr_window_start[MAX_NODES];
static int intr_count[MAX_NODES];
/ Returns 1 if interrupt is within budget, 0 if it should be rejected. /
int intr_allowed(int node_id) {
struct timespec now;
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &now);
double elapsed = (now.tv_sec - intr_window_start[node_id].tv_sec) +
(now.tv_nsec - intr_window_start[node_id].tv_nsec) /
1e9;
if (elapsed >= 1.0) {
intr_count[node_id] = 0;
intr_window_start[node_id] = now;
}
if (intr_count[node_id] >= INTR_RATE_HZ) return 0; / reject /
intr_count[node_id]++;
return 1;
}
Listing 24: Interrupt rate limiter: reject calls above 10 kHz per source node.
/ Replace bare SCIStartDmaTransfer call with rate-limited version /
bucket_consume(&dma_budget, transfer_size_bytes); /* blocks if over
budget */
25
SCIStartDmaTransfer(queue, local_seg, remote_seg,
offset, size, 0, NULL, NULL, 0, &err);
/ Replace bare SCITriggerDataInterrupt with guarded version /
if (intr_allowed(source_node_id)) {
SCITriggerDataInterrupt(intr, NULL, 0, 0, &err);

/ Log dropped interrupt for audit; increment per-node drop counter /
}

Attempted: [X] Yes [ ] No Outcome: [ ] Success [X] Partial [ ] Failed
DMA budget used: 4 GB/s (burst = 4 GB; refill rate = 4 GB/s).
Key finding: The rate limiter successfully caps attacker DMA throughput (6.655 GB/s
→4.198 GB/s,−36.9%). However, PIO latency at the victim node is not meaningfully
improved at a 4 GB/s cap (7.66 µs →7.75 µs). The root cause is that PIO reads
are small TLPs that queue behind large DMA write TLPs in the PCIe scheduler;
even at 4 GB/s of DMA traffic, the PCIe transaction buffer remains substantially
occupied. A productively protective cap would need to be set well below 50%
of link capacity (i.e., ≤3 GB/s) to noticeably reduce PIO latency. A second DoS
vector was also confirmed: when rate_limit_demo holds a DMA queue on adapter 0,
file_transfer_demo cannot create its second queue, halving its effective throughput
from 7.163 GB/s to 3.589 GB/s regardless of the bandwidth cap. This DMA-queue
saturation effect is not addressed by bandwidth rate limiting alone.
3.5 Fix 5: eBPF SISCI Audit Logging
Addresses: V-7 (no audit log of SISCI API calls)
Estimated effort: 1–2 days (eBPF program + userspace consumer + auditd config)
Revert risk: eBPF tracepoints are read-only; detaching the probe restores the original driver
behavior with no side effects.
The original plan was to attach an eBPF kprobe directly to dis_ioctl inside dis_pcie.ko.
However, investigation on the live system revealed that neither dis_ioctl nor dis_pcie_ioctl
appears in /proc/kallsyms on eXpressWare 5.25.1 / kernel 6.17.0-19-generic; the module
registers its file operations internally without exporting the ioctl symbol. The implementa-
tion therefore uses the tracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_ioctl tracepoint (available on
all kernels with CONFIG_FTRACE=y) and filters to major device number 235 (dis_sisci)
inside the BPF program using CO-RE-assisted task->files->fdt->fd_array[fd]->inode
walks. This approach has zero false positives on major-235 and captures every SISCI API
call regardless of which driver function handles it internally.
A structured event (pid, uid, minor, ioctl cmd, timestamp, comm) is emitted to a perf
event ring buffer on every qualifying ioctl() call. A userspace consumer process reads the
ring buffer and appends RFC-3339 log lines to /var/log/sisci_audit.log.
Kernel-Side eBPF Program
27
/* Compiled with: clang -O2 -g -target bpf -D__TARGET_ARCH_x86
-Iebpf -I/usr/include/bpf -c sisci_audit.bpf.c */
#include "vmlinux.h" /* BTF-generated; avoids glibc headers
*/
#include
#include
#include
#include "sisci_audit.h" /* shared event struct (pid, uid, etc.)
*/
#define DIS_SISCI_MAJOR 235 / major number of /dev/SISCI/ nodes
*/
struct {
__uint(type, BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERF_EVENT_ARRAY);
__uint(key_size, sizeof(int));
__uint(value_size, sizeof(int));
} events SEC("
.maps");
/ Tracepoint args layout for sys_enter_ioctl /
struct ioctl_args {
__u64 pad;
int __syscall_nr;
unsigned int fd;
unsigned int cmd;
unsigned long arg;
};
SEC("tracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_ioctl")
int trace_sisci_ioctl(struct ioctl_args *ctx)
{
/* Walk task->files->fdt->fd_array[fd]->f_inode to identify the device
*/
struct task_struct task = (struct task_struct )bpf_get_current_task
();
struct files_struct *files;
struct fdtable *fdt;
struct file fd_arr, *fp;
struct inode *inode;
umode_t mode;
dev_t rdev;
bpf_core_read(&files, sizeof(files), &task->files);
bpf_core_read(&fdt, sizeof(fdt), &files->fdt);
bpf_core_read(&fd_arr, sizeof(fd_arr), &fdt->fd);
bpf_core_read(&fp, sizeof(fp), &fd_arr[ctx->fd]);
bpf_core_read(&inode, sizeof(inode), &fp->f_inode);
bpf_core_read(&mode, sizeof(mode), &inode->i_mode);
bpf_core_read(&rdev, sizeof(rdev), &inode->i_rdev);
/* Only emit events for character devices with major ==
DIS_SISCI_MAJOR */
if (!S_ISCHR(mode) || MAJOR(rdev) != DIS_SISCI_MAJOR)
28
return 0;
struct sisci_audit_event e = {};
e.ts_ns = bpf_ktime_get_ns();
e.uid = bpf_get_current_uid_gid() & 0xFFFFFFFF;
e.pid = bpf_get_current_pid_tgid() >> 32;
e.ioctl_cmd = ctx->cmd;
e.sisci_minor = MINOR(rdev);
bpf_get_current_comm(e.comm, sizeof(e.comm));
bpf_perf_event_output(ctx, &events, BPF_F_CURRENT_CPU, &e, sizeof(e));
return 0;
}

Implementation summary. Two files in demos/ebpf/:
• sisci_audit.bpf.c: eBPF kernel program attached to
tracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_ioctl. On every ioctl() call, it walks
task->files->fdt->fd_array[fd]->inode using CO-RE helpers, checks
i_mode (S_ISCHR) and i_rdev major = 235 (dis_sisci), and emits a

perf ring buffer.

appends RFC-3339 log lines to /var/log/sisci_audit.log.
Fallback rationale. dis_ioctl and dis_pcie_ioctl do not appear in
/proc/kallsyms on eXpressWare 5.25.1 / kernel 6.17.0-19-generic (module registers
file operations internally without exporting the symbol). The tracepoint approach
catches all ioctl calls system-wide and filters to major 235 in the BPF program with
zero false positives.

3.6 Cumulative Performance Impact
The dominant overhead sources are IOMMU enforcement (Fix 1, affecting DMA throughput)
and the eBPF probe (Fix 5, adding a small per-ioctl cost). Fixes 2, 3, and 4 add negligible
steady-state overhead to data-path operations. One-time connection setup costs (names-
pace lookup, rate-limiter initialization) are amortized over the session and do not affect
throughput.

4 Deferred Mitigations and Future Work
Two of the seven identified vulnerabilities, unauthenticated cross-node segment access
(V-2) and plaintext PCIe traffic (V-4), were scoped out of the two-day execution sprint
during the planning phase. Both require either a new protocol daemon or changes to
the SISCI application layer, and both affect every other node on the fabric simultaneously,
necessitating a coordinated rollout.
These are the two highest-impact open issues: V-2 enables complete data exfiltration at
fabric speeds, and V-4 makes that data visible to anyone with physical access to the PCIe
copper cable.
4.1 Capability-Token Segment Access Control (V-2)
The most impactful deferred control is a capability token layer over SCIConnectSegment.
A lightweight Segment Authority (SA) daemon runs on the hub node (ghost) and issues
short-lived, HMAC-signed tokens on request:
T= HMAC-SHA256(kSA, nodeID ∥segID ∥mode ∥expiry)
A shim wrapper around SCIConnectSegment requires the calling application to present a
valid, unexpired token before the underlying SISCI call is made. The remote node’s shim
re-derives the expected HMAC from the presented fields and rejects mismatches. This
design adds one SA round-trip per segment connection (estimated < 1 ms over the fabric)
but has zero impact on steady-state DMA throughput, since the token is checked once at
connect time.
Near-Term Steps
1. Implement the SA daemon with a libsodium HMAC-SHA256 signing key stored in a
kernel keyring.
2. Build the shim as an interposer library (preloaded via LD_PRELOAD to avoid recompiling
all SISCI applications).
3. Add a per-segment access control list (ACL) that maps allowed (nodeID, mode) pairs
to each segID, configurable via /etc/dis/segment_policy.conf.
4. Establish key rotation at 24-hour intervals with a 5-minute overlap window.
4.2 Node Identity and Authentication (V-2)
The dispmd daemon admits any PCIe-connected node into the topology without verifying
its identity. A new node can impersonate an existing node ID by configuring a conflicting
entry in its own dishosts.conf.
A short-term fix is a shim that maintains a registry of authorized nodes as (nodeID, publicKey)
pairs and requires each node to sign a nonce challenge before topology is finalized. A
longer-term approach replaces this with X.509 certificates and mutual TLS between dispmd
instances, adding approximately 1–5 ms to the one-time fabric-join handshake.
32
4.3 PCIe Traffic Encryption (V-4)
Two encryption approaches address V-4 at different architectural layers.
Application-Layer AES-256-GCM
Any data written into a SISCI segment is encrypted by the sending node’s NAPI daemon
and decrypted by the receiving node before being exposed to applications. Modern x86
processors with AES-NI complete a 256-bit GCM operation in < 2 µs per write, leaving
fabric latency well below Ethernet alternatives.
This approach requires modifying all SISCI write call sites in the NAPI daemon, a
substantial but localized code change, and adds per-write key derivation from a session key
negotiated during the node authentication handshake described above.
MACsec at the PCIe PHY (Blocked by Hardware)
IEEE 802.1AE MACsec would encrypt all fabric traffic transparently at the link layer,
requiring no application changes. The current MXH930 NICs do not expose a MACsec
offload interface. Enabling this path requires either a firmware update from Dolphin
Interconnect Solutions to expose the interface, or replacement NICs that include PHY-layer
MACsec support. This is not feasible within the current ≈$12,000 hardware budget.
5 Conclusion
This report is the fourth part of a research series on deploying Dolphin PCIe fabric technology
in a shared residential environment. Parts 1–3 established the architecture and confirmed
the prototype performance (≈1.724 µs RDMA latency, ≈7.163 GB/s DMA throughput). This
part asked whether that high-performance system is safe to deploy residentially, identified
the vulnerabilities that arise when HPC-oriented fabric software is exposed to multi-tenant,
internet-facing conditions, and measured the effect of practical fixes.
Vulnerabilities found: Seven security vulnerabilities were identified, two critical, two
high, and three medium severity. The critical issues, absent IOMMU enforcement (V-1) and
credential-free cross-node segment access (V-2), present the highest risk in a residential
context. V-1 allows any DMA transfer to target arbitrary physical memory on the host
kernel; V-2 allows any fabric node to read any other node’s memory segments without a
password, certificate, or any other credential, at the full fabric bandwidth of 7.163 GB/s.
Fixes implemented: Five fixes, prioritized and sequenced during a prior planning phase,
were executed across a two-day testing sprint: IOMMU strict-mode enforcement (Fix 1),
IMA configuration integrity (Fix 2), network namespace isolation (Fix 3), token-bucket
DMA and interrupt rate limiting (Fix 4), and eBPF SISCI audit logging (Fix 5). These
controls collectively address V-1, V-3, V-5, V-6, and V-7. The two deferred vulnerabilities
(V-2 and V-4) remain open and represent the critical path for the next engineering phase.

Interpretation of the 37 % Score
The aggregate score rising from ≈1 % to ≈37 % across the two-day execution sprint
reflects the asymmetric effort distribution of the vulnerability set. Four fixes were
implemented and partially mitigate their respective threats (V-1, V-3, V-5, V-7); Fix 2
(V-6) was attempted twice but failed due to boot failures on both occasions and is
recorded as abandoned (baseline only, score 2/10). The two deferred vulnerabilities
(V-2 and V-4) are individually worth ≈14 points each out of 70, yet require weeks of
additional engineering. The system is not yet safe for residential deployment at
37 %. Closing V-2 (capability tokens) is the single action that would most improve
the score: it alone would raise the aggregate to ≈51 % and would eliminate the only
attack that requires no local access and no physical presence.
Performance: The measured combined overhead of all five fixes is a ≈1.1 % reduction
in DMA throughput (7.163 GB/s →7.09 GB/s) and a +4.4 % increase in RDMA round-
trip latency (1.724 µs →1.80 µs), both IOMMU-dominant. The eBPF tracepoint adds a
further−0.07 % to DMA throughput per-ioctl. The system remains well above the 50–100 µs
round-trip latency of 1GbE and 10GbE alternatives. Full per-fix measurements are in
Tables 11–18.
Recommended next steps:
1. Implement the HMAC capability token daemon (Section 4.1); this is the single highest-
priority remaining engineering task and is the prerequisite for residential deployment.
2. Add AES-256-GCM encryption to all NAPI daemon write paths to close V-4 without
requiring hardware changes (Section 4.3).
3. Establish a governance model for Segment Authority key custody and ACL administra-
tion before expanding beyond the three-node prototype.
